en: **Preface to the Verses on the Causality and Realization of the Sixteen Arhats** I have once perused the Great Canon of the Buddhist Teachings and investigated the principles of all virtues.

I observed how the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas exert the power of vast compassion and open the gates of beneficial skillful means— ranging from the great elements of heaven, earth, mountains, and rivers, down to the smallest insects.

The myriad species of grasses and trees serve as excellent metaphors for awakening deluded followers; yet alas, karmic fetters form such deep and lofty obstructions that those who cling to evil and remain ignorant of the good are many, while those who perceive their nature and recognize the mind are few.
Therefore, Buddha after Buddha left behind instructions, and patriarch after patriarch transmitted words, to rescue all living beings and fulfill the Great Vow.
Thus, according to the categories within the volumes, the expositions of the various sages were compiled in their entirety as the Great Canon.
In total, there were four hundred and eighty cases comprising five thousand forty-eight fascicles, which I have recorded and cataloged so that they might not fall into neglect or loss.
During the Qingli era, when I served as a Minister of State, the Western Qiang rebelled against our benevolence and incited disturbances along the borders;

the Emperor, wearying his armies and distressing his people to exterminate these wicked foes, took pity upon the common folk and the officers, and commanded me to serve as Pacification Commissioner for Hedong and its border regions.
While traveling along the road, I stayed overnight at the Bao-de Binggu Inn.
There, I happened to find a scroll of an old scripture between the cracks of the hall’s eaves; it was titled *The Verses on the Cognition of Cause and Effect*.

The characters were all written in ancient clerical script (*lishu*), a work not recorded in the Tripitaka and rarely heard of in the world. I was quite surprised by this, so I unrolled the scroll and examined it.
This is the hymn on the Great Dharma of Awakening to the Source through the Realization of Causality, Consciousness, and Perception as taught by the Buddha,
recited for Maṇirata and others by sixteen great Arhats of the Sixteen Kingdoms. One verse per honored one, totaling one hundred and twelve verses,
all directly point to the source of birth and death, deeply expound the methods of the mind-nature, and open up the true illumination of samādhi and prajñā.
This preface on the gradual dharma of eliminating the poison of the afflictive hindrances, saving sentient beings by prohibiting killing and encouraging goodness while expelling heterodoxy;

and this exposition of the four immeasurable virtues and the sudden teaching that presents the dharma-gate of non-duality: though the sudden and gradual differ, they are no different in benefiting those of sharp and dull faculties.
May the various demons and the three evil realms not arise in the mind, and may all dharmas and conditions alike return to goodness. I.
With every phrase, sigh, verse, and awakening, until the end of the scroll, my mind was suddenly cleared and I realized that there was great significance in worldly conditions;
had it not been for the World-Honored One—a Sage whose six supernormal powers and myriad practices are perfectly luminous and who possesses sublime discernment—I could never have reached this point.
Only now do I know that within the mundane world there are boundless holy dharmas, and that within the Great Canon there exists [this treasure].
The *Bequeathed Jewel Text* was respectfully entrusted to the monks of Chengtian Monastery in Fu Prefecture, where it was separately recorded and preserved.
Subsequently, when shown to various eminent lecturers, realized masters, and renowned scholars, none had previously seen or heard of it; all were filled with reverence and faith.
Later, in the year Wuzi, an elderly monk named Hui-zhe from Jiangling came to visit. While conversing, he spoke of this verse, which is a secret of the various sages.
This work is a secret that has rarely been heard of in the world; Master Que transmitted it to Sengpuhuan of Wuling, where it was treasured for over thirty years before another copy was encountered.
I, therefore, sought out a duplicate to correct its errors and discrepancies, intending to present it to Shen Zhi.
Thus, I have directly recorded these matters to document its origins. Preface by Fan Zhongyan of Gaoping, during the second month of spring in the year Wuzi.
Verses on the Causal and Resultant Cognitions of the Sixteen Great Arhats,
translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Jñānagupta.
At that time, the sixteen Great Arhats of the various kingdoms were listening to the Buddha’s teaching beneath the Pi-zi-qi musical tree.
After the great Dharma assembly on the realization that one is originally a Buddha through the awakening to the consciousness of cause and effect concluded, they returned with joy;
their natures and minds were suddenly enlightened, and all attained the fruit of Buddhahood. At that time, all the Great Arhats assembled upon the Terrace of Accumulated Jewels in Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
There were one hundred and fifty bhikṣu monks, including Maṇirata and others, who heard these [words].

Having heard the Buddha’s exposition of the Great Dharma of realizing one's original Buddhahood through the awakening to causal consciousness and perception, the Arhats returned and gathered beneath the platform.
Surrounding him with reverence and making prostrations with deep devotion, they addressed the great Arhats, saying:

"Throughout successive kalpas we have practiced cultivation, exclusively upholding the precepts and meditative concentration, yet we have never seen a Buddha nor heard the True Dharma. Now that we have heard it from the assembly of the Holy Ones..."

Having heard the Buddha’s discourse on the Great Dharma of the causal consciousness that awakens to the fundamental nature and attains Buddhahood, we now humbly beseech all the Sages for their great compassion and pity;
may they expound it for us so that we may attain the correct fruit. At that time, the Venerable Nakula said:
"You have only recently entered the stream of the sages and have not yet escaped birth and death. Although you possess the fruits of goodness, you remain attached to them, and thus..."
"Those who have not yet awakened find it difficult to see the Buddha; we have seen the causal consciousness that perceives the Great Dharma of attaining Buddhahood.
When each of us has individually attained awakening and realized the fruit of Bodhi," Maṇirada again addressed the Venerable Ones:

"What is meant by 'causal consciousness that perceives'? The Venerable Ones replied: "'Cause' refers to causes and conditions; 'fruit' refers to karmic retribution; 'consciousness' refers to the original mind itself; and 'perception' refers to—"
"Seeing its original nature, if there are good karmic fruits and blessings arising from causes and conditions, one will naturally recognize one's own fundamental mind.
By seeing this original nature so that the myriad dharmas do not arise, one shall attain Buddhahood. Maṇirata addressed the Venerable One again:

"The causes and conditions, the fruits and retributions, and the lightness or gravity of good and evil—please, Venerable One, explain these for us. The Venerable One said: "Listen attentively, and I shall speak for you."

What you have said—that one who utters kind words is not equal to one who generates a wholesome mind, and one who generates a wholesome mind is not equal to one who performs wholesome deeds—is because:
one who utters kind words has the cause for merit; one who generates a wholesome mind has the basis for merit;
and one who performs wholesome deeds has the fruition of merit. Therefore, one who utters evil words is lighter [in consequence] than one who...
One who gives rise to an evil mind is light in committing evil deeds. Why is this? One who utters evil words has a cause for transgression;
one who gives rise to an evil mind has a basis for transgression; one who commits evil deeds has a retribution for transgression.
Thus, when karmic results correspond to their causes, they are like shadows following forms or weights on a scale, not differing by even a hair’s breadth. Maṇava.

When Rādha and the others heard what the Venerable One had said, they were filled with single-minded reverence and addressed him repeatedly, saying, "We pray that you will preach the Great Dharma to deliver those who have not yet awakened.
The Venerable One replied, "It is by these causes and conditions that we have reached this time.

Then each of the sixteen great Arhats reflected upon their own thoughts and, for the sake of Rādha and the others, transmitted the knowledge of cause and effect and the realization of the fundamental nature, whereby they attained enlightenment.
The Buddha’s Great Dharma consists of seven verses for each section, totaling one hundred and twelve verses.
First, the account of the Venerable Bharadvāja clarifies the principles of good and evil; the retribution of hidden merits is as level as a scale.
I have composed these one hundred verses on cause and effect, Expounding the Dharma-nature to bestow wisdom upon sentient beings.
Having severed all desires of the desire realm and never returning again, This solitary spirit soars upward to the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven;
Forever eliminating afflictions and departing from birth and death, One finally attains the complete fruit of the Anāgāmin path.
Gradual and sudden methods are not two kinds; at the time of attaining the Way, the principle is one and the same.
Whether dull or sharp, fast or slow, these arise from what is perceived. Each manifests spiritual powers according to their own fundamental nature.
Exhausting filial piety in the family and exhausting loyalty in the state—the methods for governing the family and governing the state are both fully understood.
Not yet knowing where one's life and nature shall return, One must ask the Tathāgata about suffering and emptiness.
The world’s scales, measures, and bushels Can cause your mind to give rise to resentment;
Just look at those who seek profit in this way— How many will live to see their hair turn white?
The body is the Sangha and the mind is the Sangha; when body and mind are both clearly understood, one is a true monk.
Unstained by worldly conditions and free from affliction—who else could equal such a monk?
I bestow upon you the Dharma-seal to stabilize the single mind; I bestow upon you the Dharma-power to capture the six thieves.
When the mind is settled, the thief is extinguished and true nature shines; this causes your Dharmakāya to be eternally attained of itself.
Second, Venerable Kanakavatsa:
the Buddha-way is impartial, opening ten thousand gates; the nature of all sentient beings is ever-present.
If you can give rise to a single thought of pure faith, You shall behold the World-Honored One in the heavens or among men.

With the two hundred and fifty precepts of pure conduct, And the constant practice of the Four Noble Truths, You will personally receive the blessings of devas and humans through the six supernormal powers; This is the cause for the noble fruit of Arhatship.
One’s nature is like the autumn moon illuminating all quarters; Desire is like floating clouds that painfully obscure it.
Once the wind of wisdom blows them away, The clear sky reveals the light of the single orb.
Practice with urgency, practice with urgency! Seventy years of life have passed like a flowing stream.
You are able to eliminate all evils through the principle of nature; It is not enough merely to don the black robes and shave the head.

One hundred and twenty minus twenty, And one hundred further reduced by thirty years— As the kalpas gradually fill and human life becomes increasingly brief, Even seventy years now is considered difficult to attain.
In vain you employ Chan theories with such flourish, Your mouth eloquently explains while your practice remains unformed.
That no dharma can be spoken is precisely the Way; The roots of goodness do not arise from one’s own words.
I bestow upon you the Dharma-gate to open all obscurations; I bestow upon you the Dharma-path to lead all who are lost.
The obscured is clarified and the mind’s penetration made fully clear; It causes your Dharma-body to be free from doubt.
Third, Venerable Nāgabodhi:
you have attained human birth and preserved your Buddha-nature; All things revolve like a wheel from external conditions.
If you can transform objects and maintain true nature, You are the Tathāgata’s body of realized awakening.
With nothing to be attained within and nothing to be sought without, The source of the pure mind encompasses all practices;
When desire and lust do not arise, afflictions are severed. The World-Honored One’s wondrous intent lies in diligent cultivation.
Throughout the day one makes offerings seeking fields of merit, yet fails to seek the source of liberation from birth and death;
instead, one takes such blessings as true virtue. Though one performs meritorious deeds, there is no way thereby to see the root of one's nature.
Whether one is wealthy or poor has its own causes; since past conditions and karmic allotments are fixed, do not strive against them with force.
Having never sown seeds in the springtime, One sits idly guarding a wasteland, hoping for an autumn harvest.
Illness, legal punishment, and death; Isolation, poverty, and distress—how truly frantic!
If you can skillfully bestow grace and wisdom, How would this differ from practicing the fasts and establishing a dharma-hall?
Having attained seventy-one hundred [years], you have created boundless karmic offenses.
Do not wait for virtuous fruits; turn your mind back early! When will you change your appearance and depart?
I grant you the Dharma-boat to cross the sea of suffering; I grant you the Dharma-wind to sweep away the dust of karma.
Crossing the sea, the dust is cleared as you reach the other shore; May you awaken your Dharma-body to the ultimate truth.
The Fourth, Venerable Subhūti:
tongue, body, nose, eyes, and mind are all acute; Yet the six thieves run wild, throwing the nature-source into chaos.
You maintain the precepts and cultivate both concentration and wisdom; By means of these three dharmas, you extinguish all ferocities.
The existence within space is formless in nature; Suddenly it is assigned to a physical body.
If one allows the physical form to give rise to delusive thoughts And fails to seek the primordial nature, this is ignorance.
The lotus root is planted beneath the mud; receiving its vital energy, it secretly sprouts buds as the seasons turn.
Gradually drawing forth stalks and stems until they rise above the water’s surface, only then can the multitude behold the lotus flower.
Blessings arise naturally from one's own goodness—there is no other path; calamity results from the accumulation of evil, according to the natural law.
Clearly manifest, the fruits of retribution do not err; Alas, how can the ignorant and deluded fail to reform themselves?
At the moment of death, a thousandfold sufferings arise, As karmic creditors draw one away and bring one back again.
If one remains unimpeded by worldly attachments, Then one may leave the human realm as swiftly as a finger-snap.
When fortune and power prevail, people vie to be close; When fortune and power depart, people vie to be malicious.
While you possess fortune and power, Cultivate the excellent path ahead for yourself.
I bestow upon you the Dharma-incense to remove defilement, And I bestow upon you the Dharma-seat to stabilize your nature.
Defilements are eliminated and the nature of meditative concentration is spontaneously perfected and luminous; It causes your Dharma-body to remain eternally pure.
The fifth, Venerable Nāgārjuna, is born wherever he may be, all of which is the Way; At that moment, all is extinguished and returns to emptiness.
Completely free from hindrance, the mind is pure; Suddenly awakening to perfect luminosity, it penetrates everywhere.
Internally perceiving one’s own nature, it is exceptionally unmoving; Externally observing all objects, they are likewise non-existent.
With neither internal attachment nor external clinging, One suddenly awakens to True Suchness from this point on.
Samādhi is the moon and wisdom is its light; The essence and function of the moonlight conceal all evils within the nature of reality.
To see the Buddha, look within one’s own nature and seek nothing outside; Taking refuge, I constantly burn incense of faith.
The sun, moon, mountains, and rivers all have their end; Yet that which has form perishes while the principle remains eternal.
Few are those who tread the path to Bodhi; they do not realize that the years of their life pass like flashes of lightning.

Though heaven and earth provide the means for food, clothing, and shelter, sustaining all living beings and fulfilling every need, they fail to give rise to a virtuous mind and thus waste much in vain.
As they transmigrate through the six realms of existence, their retribution knows no rest.
Reflect upon the events of your past lives; wealth, nobility, and splendor are but a single dream.
Failing to realize that birth and death are matters of great consequence, your body is finite while your affairs are endless.
I bestow upon you the Wheel of Dharma to turn away the three poisons; I bestow upon you the wisdom of Dharma to purify a hundred defilements.
Poison eliminated and defilements exhausted, he dwells in self-concealment and peace; May you achieve the realization of the Dharma-body.
The sixth, Venerable Bhadra, took fundamental desire as his root; Afflictions have followed him ever since.
Yet, by severing the bonds of desire, Afflictions naturally cease and one no longer wanders in saṃsāra.
Constantly illuminating one's nature with wisdom, The mind does not give rise to any kind of evil karma;
Even when wholesome thoughts arise, one remains unattached, And the wondrous fruit of Bodhi naturally deepens.

Bodhi and prajñā are true wisdom; the innate mind of the nature of worldly beings is deluded and fails to awaken to the intent of the Tathāgata. When seeking it outside of oneself, there is no end in sight;
if one does not cultivate wholesome causes and virtuous conditions, one will suffer the daily torment of craving fame and profit.
Who would have known that the gold, silver, and treasures remaining in the world were lent to you for seventy years of leisurely viewing?
People of this world merely resent the suffering of hunger and cold; these [treasures] are all spent in vain.
If one maintains the Middle Way and practices constant frugality, then clothing and food will naturally become abundant.
Your mind dwells upon thoughts of glory and wealth; you imagine the abundance of music, women, pearls, and gold, following your whims with pleasure according to your desires.
Yet, what difference is there between such a life and that of a common mortal?
I grant you the Dharma-fan to dispel evil delusions; I grant you the Dharma-jewel to restrain greed and desire.
When greed and delusion do not arise, the sense faculties are purified; this causes your Dharma-body to be eternally self-sufficient.
The seventh, the Venerable Kali, whose body is threefold and mouth fourfold, yet whose mind encompasses all three—do not indulge in the ten evils that follow the person.
If you do not awaken even while facing this, what more can you hope for regarding the nature of phenomena?
All worldly afflictions and deluded thoughts cannot invade one's own original nature.
The noble person is without self or false views; the source of birth and cessation resides entirely within the mind.
Externally deluded by attachment to forms, internally deluded by emptiness; The gates are blocked and the paths do not pass through.
To be free from form within form is true form; To be free from emptiness within emptiness is true emptiness.
Bound and entangled by craving and desire, one sinks without end; Afflictions arise daily and follow one constantly.
Even when the state's prisons remain open for amnesty, The family estate is seized and imprisoned even when the time for pardon arrives.

When insects and birds take advantage of spring to lay eggs and raise their young, If one destroys their nests and takes their offspring—there is no difference between these beings in their love and nurturing;
Once they have become enemies in life and death, they will surely seek retribution.
Always teach those who desire [the path] to distance themselves from what is before their eyes; Let the six sense faculties not be dragged by karmic conditions.
Gradually upholding and gradually precepting, one realizes the true nature; Only when the mind is absent toward sensory objects is the Way complete.
I bestow upon you the Dharma-scale to weigh out the impurities of anger; I bestow upon you the Dharma-bell to awaken the deafness of ignorance.
Hatred ceases, delusion awakens, and all virtues arise; may this bring you inexhaustible bliss in the Dharmakāya. (8) Venerable Puṇṇa:
"The mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the mind; if you harbor the mind, you will find no Buddha outside of it."
One further knows that both good and evil are created by the mind; The principle of the Tathāgata is seen to be profoundly deep.
The original nature of human life is entirely pure; All phenomena arise from their own inherent nature.
When the nature of the mind accords with itself, there is no movement; Luminously clear, internal and external are naturally distinct.
Consciousness arises from the fundamental mind, its own nature; Neither born nor extinguished, it is entirely free from contention.
In all times, it penetrates all things; Suchness is unmoving and eternally pure.
Those who in this life possess the fortune of dwelling in honor and wealth, Have had the causal conditions from past lives—this principle does not err.
Furthermore, one seeks to augment merit within the field of merit; thus, the rewards of merit will be boundless throughout successive lives.
A pellet from a hand-cannon and a sticky rice ball—each innocent life slain beyond the realm of things, each grievance, shall receive its retribution.
In the darkness, these karmic enemies follow one another.
With a concentrated mind, you calmly contemplate the nature of all phenomena;
They possess no dual characteristics, being each definitively like the vast, open sky. Above and below, there is no obstruction; all is pure and serene.
May you be granted the Dharma-vajra to strike down the hosts of Māras, And may you be granted the Dharma-cloud to shroud all cravings.
Māra is subdued, craving severed, and the physical body made empty; This allows your Dharma-body to be free from all obstruction.
Venerable Śubhaka, ninth in the sequence:
Because you dispelled darkness, you waited for the dawn; Yet when the light fades, the darkness arises once more.
If you wish to attain eternal illumination and remove the veil of darkness, simply hold fast to the torch of wisdom and practice it constantly.
You have realized that the physical body has no permanent abode; you must clearly understand that the fundamental nature is the true refuge.
A single lamp dispels the darkness of a thousand years, illuminating the hall and kitchen as entirely illusory.
One transformation brings about the bliss of rebirth in the heavens; Another transformation brings about the suffering of rebirth in hell.
Both transformations arise from within one's own nature. To what realm do you intend to go through your transformations?
Do not treat lightly the lives of sentient beings; Loving life and detesting killing is the nature of all things.
You crave the hundred flavors of pungent and tainted delicacies; you hear the cries of sentient beings being led to slaughter.
Your parents’ remains lie in shallow earth—hurry to perform their burial without delay.
Do not linger in doubt while seeking worldly blessings; otherwise, you shall not escape becoming a sinner before the Lord of the Underworld.
The body itself is signless yet undergoes birth; the mind arises and ceases because of the presence of objects.
If there were no external objects, the mind would not exist of its own accord. The nature of the mind is lucid—how is it different from a Buddha?
I bestow upon you the Dharma-stand to transcend form and appearance; I bestow upon you the Dharma-sword to quell all fear.
Seeing the extinction of fear through separation from appearances is the fundamental tenet; it causes your Dharmakāya to be non-dual.
(10th Half) The Venerable Nāgabodhi’s mind is a clear mirror, while desire is the dust. When the dust is thick, the clarity within is obscured; this is the cause for its disappearance.
Gradually departing and gradually polishing away, when the floating impurities are exhausted, One naturally attains penetrating illumination of the mental activities of those coming and going.
The mouth speaks of emptiness while the body maintains good and evil; This duality constitutes one's own delusion and attachment.
For ten thousand kalpas, there will be no way to perceive the source of the nature.
Earth, water, fire, and wind transform this body; when the body perishes, the four great elements each return to their source.
All demons and the six thieves are utterly dispersed; suffering and joy are but the guest in the house of the future.
Widowers, widows, orphans, and the solitary—these four classes of people suffer no pain from being destitute, for they are already in a state of hunger and poverty.
You are able to deliver others through wisdom and maintain compassion; This supreme orientation toward Bodhi is a root of goodness.
Free from resentment and ignorance, you maintain a mind of patience and equanimity toward all things;
When others come with evil, you respond with goodness. Profoundly realizing samādhi, you are named "The One Without Conflict."
Broadly opening the mind’s capacity to its boundless limits, The mountains and rivers of all worlds are entirely contained within it;
Without right or wrong, and free from attachment, May you always make the mind equal to the great void.
I grant you the Bridge of Dharma to rescue those in distress and peril; I grant you the Sash of Dharma to resolve enmity and resentment.
Calamities and enmities are extinguished and nothing remains to bind you; It causes your Dharma-body to return to spontaneity.
(11) Venerable Rāhula, the six thieves are purified and there is no affliction;
Since afflictions have no time [of existence], wisdom is naturally luminous.
Illuminately seeing that all conditions are external things, They are one and the same as the principle of Heaven—merely empty and pure.
Sitting in stillness with an empty mind is not for the sake of emptiness;
If one says the Way is neither empty nor non-empty, it is like the void encompassing the myriad phenomena. Only this kind of emptiness is truly the "emptiness of emptiness."
The end of good and evil is like accumulated water; Through the flow and the dew, it gradually becomes deep.
When good is deep, one naturally obtains immeasurable blessings; How can one avoid the encroachment of calamity when evil has accumulated?
When seeing others in distress, danger, or exhaustion, One should employ skillful means and perform secret meritorious deeds to rescue them.
Among causes and effects, this is the foremost: Through the merit of conditions, the Buddha’s Bodhi is realized and arises of itself.
From youth to old age, and from old age to sickness, And from sickness to death—the suffering is immeasurable.
Unable to gradually awaken to the principle of saṃsāra, There is no way to escape the calamities of birth and death.
If your mind turns toward the Buddha, the Buddha naturally perceives you; if your mind turns away from the Buddha, the Buddha naturally has no perception of you.
When you turn toward the Buddha, all manner of goodness naturally arises; when you turn away from the Buddha, all manner of evil naturally pursues you.
I grant you the staff of Dharma to repent for past transgressions; I grant you the script of Dharma to confess prior evils.
Transgressions and evils are examined and reformed, yet one remains naturally composed;
thus your Dharma-body has nothing to which it clings. (12) Venerable Nāgasena’s realm:
if consciousness excels, all roots of goodness are known; if consciousness can excel its objects, the myriad conditions are penetrated.
Internally and externally, with no attachment to objects; this very state is emptiness, yet there is no further "emptiness-nature" to be found.
The mind is settled, the body is settled, and they are naturally settled. At the time of liberation, there is nothing to strive for;
coming, going, and staying are simply the ordinary. Transmitted from master to master, all take refuge herein.
If there are karmic grudges from past lives or this life, you must repay them through merit;
once all debts from the past have been settled, you shall depart from the world with clear accounts rendered.
If you seek to realize the fruit of enlightenment under the Tathāgata, you must rely upon the Triple Gem to increase your wholesome conditions.
If one can practice pure filial piety toward one's parents, how is this different from reading sutras and feeding the sangha?
Yet you crave banquets and call it joy; how many kinds of sentient beings have you slaughtered among the waters and lands?
You still lament that the hundred varieties of pungent and stinking meats are not enough—try calculating the number of living creatures you have consumed and see for yourself.
If you seek to cultivate the true nature of all Buddhas, first direct your mind toward wholesome states within all conditions.
Gradually awaken to the luminosity of this nature, and all objective realms will cease. You shall naturally penetrate the Buddha-nature deeply;
I now bestow upon you the objects of all dharmas. Hold fast to these objects, and you shall sever all malevolent spirits and demons.
When evil is extinguished and demons eliminated, one shall see one's true nature; naturally, merit will fill the Ganges.
(13) Because the Venerable Kātyāyana’s nature and mind were in accord, evil could not enter him; his resolve was united with the Way, and his consciousness was entirely clear.
One completely parts from the six sense objects and the five desires; From this, the fruit of Bodhi is realized.
A single jar of nectar irrigates the field of the mind; The fire of karma turns to ash, suddenly and brilliantly clear.
Suddenly encountering one's original nature within purity, Together one soars upward to the Tuṣita Heaven.
Do not kill, do not steal, and do not commit sexual misconduct; these three virtues of the body are the very limit of blessings.
When the source of the mind is clear and all faculties are pure, what need is there to seek out mountains or leave the household life?
If someone harms you, you must respond; for every going and coming, there is a cause.
If you can still your mind so that it does not waver, all your karmic offenses will vanish and your true nature will be fully revealed.

Universally bestowing wholesome benefits to save all living beings, with vast compassion equal and impartial, practice giving that is perfect, pervasive, and free from the mark of abiding. How sublime is the Bodhisattva path—may you always practice it!
Your craving for fame and profit is groundless; Like a dream, you drive this finite body about.
Failing to understand how to withdraw the head and seek the path out, You vainly indulge in sinful karma, becoming but dust and ash.
I bestow upon you the water of Dharma to extinguish the fires of karma; I bestow upon you the rain of Dharma to give rise to roots of goodness.
The fire extinguished, wholesome states arise, and the mind becomes pure; It causes you to behold the World-Honored One within your Dharma-body.
(14) Venerable Vaṇavāsi has gone to the end of all dust and washed away all blemish; He is as bright as the full moon shining across the horizon.
Unmoved by all errors and devoid of form or sign, this path to the Tathāgata is not remote.

The Mahāprajñāpāramitā—wherein the principle of nature and the principle of mind are supreme—is without abiding, without going, and without coming; from it all Buddhas of the three periods of time emerge.
The future is difficult to fathom through thought; the past is not worth recounting.
Relying solely on what is before one’s eyes as the present, afflictions naturally do not follow.
Between the two matters of killing and debt, the karmic retribution for killing is the deepest of all sins.
Bestow kindness by releasing captive creatures to repay your debts; thus you may avoid drifting and sinking in the three evil realms.
Do not abandon minor virtues because they seem insignificant, for when accumulated, they become a powerful force for merit.
Do not treat minor evils as trivial matters, for as minor evils increase, they will bring about great calamity.
By practicing, one attains the fruits of the human and celestial realms; heavenly flowers and celestial music come of their own accord to welcome you to the Tuṣita Heaven.

Maitreya shall then preach the Dharma of the Superior Rebirth, bestowing upon you the lamp of Dharma to shatter all darkness, and bestowing upon you the mirror of Dharma to illuminate all transgressions.
Darkness vanishes and sins are extinguished, suddenly revealing clarity; It causes your Dharma-body to be eternally sovereign.
(15) Venerable Āśvaghosa, whose myriad practices are universally penetrating, can awaken to the nature; He drives away afflictions and cultivates with even greater diligence.
Only after seven births and seven deaths does one achieve the Way; At the initial stage of Srotāpanna, one enters the stream of the sages.
If the preceding thought has not yet realized awakening, sinful karma is formed; If the succeeding thought skillfully realizes awakening, all sins are extinguished.
Now, moment after moment, every thought dwells in emptiness; Brilliant wisdom is like the bright moon.
Among all wholesome fruits of myriad conditions, none equal filial piety; among sinful karmas, none are deeper than unfiliality.
If you clarify good and evil within this context, you will naturally accord with the heart of the Buddha-King.
As you gradually encounter swallows, sparrows, turtles, and turtles, do not begrudge your funds to purchase them and set them free.
Repaying the debts of this life’s excesses so as not to be followed by dark karmic creditors;
Firmly maintaining the precepts to eliminate all evils—though the body remains at home, the mind is that of a monk.
What need is there to leave the household life to see the Way? With the mind clearly realized within, one awakens to the Three Vehicles.
Spontaneous music provides boundless delight; The towers of the seven treasures are as magnificent as the sun and dawn clouds.
Exquisite fragrances never dissipate; Amidst the clouds, celestial flowers fall in profusion.
I grant you the Dharma-sword to sever afflictions; I grant you the Dharma-key to unlock the prison bars.
When afflictions do not arise, the shackles are released; this allows your Dharma-body to realize the fruit.
(Verse 16) Note: Although the venerable Cūḍapanthaka was nearing the completion of his meritorious practice, he still traveled back and forth—once to heaven and once to the human realm.
Only then can one realize the stage of Arhat; this is called the Srotāpanna who has crossed the barrier.
To regard giving as merit is superficial; to see into one's nature as merit is the true cause of goodness.
Because it involves dwelling in signs, this is clearly termed "merit" (puṇya).
All things arise from conditions and have their opposites; know that the distinctions between death and life, honor and disgrace, all stem from the mind.
When the field of the mind is naturally vast, there is no sorrow or affliction; one need not fear boiling water, fire, weapons, or the blade.
Yet, while seeking myriad paths to profit for oneself, one secretly lays traps and pitfalls to ensnare others.
Behold these who call themselves capable; as for their karmic retribution, who among their descendants will not have their hearts remain attached to the home?
Their bodies may leave the household, yet they do not eliminate their various evils while wearing the *kāṣāya*.
Such karmic obstacles are like the Ganges River; do not lament within the mire of the three evil realms.
Through various excellent conditions and profound parables, I extensively bestow verbal teachings to shatter the delusions and darkness of sentient beings.
Listen attentively and all take refuge with faith; The Tathāgata speaks not falsely.
I grant you the Dharma-hoe to uproot the seeds of evil, And grant you the Dharma-field to grow the sprouts of goodness.
Evil exhausted and goodness perfected, spiritual merit attained, you shall cause your Dharma-body to roam in liberation.

Thus, when the sixteen great Arhats had finished composing these verses on the Great Dharma of the Buddha’s causes and effects, the realization of consciousness and vision, and the attainment of Buddhahood for Maṇirata, they further said: "All that we have versified was the golden mouth of the World-Honored One himself."

This is the proclamation that awakens all the sages, enabling them to realize the fruits of enlightenment and attain Buddhahood; I now record it and compose it as a verse for the sake of future awakening.
You should take this verse, which identifies cause and effect through insight, as its title.

Furthermore, because the sentient beings of the world turn their backs on the good and incline toward evil, becoming deeply deluded and attached, I bestow this true verse, which shall circulate among humanity during the final kalpa.
I exhort you all to reverently uphold [this teaching] to deliver sentient beings and enable them to escape the suffering of birth and death.
Expound it widely so as to awaken future students, ensuring that all who possess discernment may, upon seeing these wondrous words, realize the fruit of enlightenment.
At that time, Maṇḍarava heard these verses of instruction from the sixteen great Arhats of the sixteen kingdoms; through their awakening, he was suddenly released from his delusions and attachments.
With a mind clearly awakened, he paid respectful homage with deep faith; after prostrating for a long time, he withdrew.
This concludes the *Verses on the Causality and Realization of the Sixteen Great Arhats*.
Attached: The Sacred Traces of the Sixteen Great Arhats (detailed in the *Dharmasthitigāthā*).
In Sanskrit, *arhat* translates in Chinese as "one beyond training" (*wuxue*), meaning that their cycle of birth and death has been exhausted and there is no further dharma to be learned.

It is also called "no-birth" (*wusheng*), meaning that having severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), they will no longer undergo rebirth within the three realms.
It is also called "worthy of offerings" (*yingsong*), meaning they are worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans. It is also called "slayer of thieves" (*shazhai*), meaning that they...

Because they are able to slay the thieves of affliction and possess the three types of higher knowledge (*traividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and immeasurable merit, they are called "Great.
These Arhats, having received the Buddha’s command, employ their supernormal powers to prolong their own lifespans and remain in the world to protect the True Dharma;
even to this day, they have not yet entered parinirvāṇa. If one should encounter...

When the world holds great, unrestricted assemblies for giving (*mahā-dāna-mahāpariṣad*), they conceal their noble appearance along with their retinues and blend in with ordinary people to receive offerings in secret, thereby enabling the donors to obtain superior karmic rewards and benefiting sentient beings;

these are the sixteen Great Arhats. (The three types of clear knowledge [*vidyā*] are: the clear knowledge of the divine eye, the clear knowledge of past lives, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. The six supernormal powers [*abhijñā*] are...)

[The six supernormal powers are] the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of others' minds, the power of psychic travel, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows).
First is the Venerable Pindola Bharadvāja: *Pindola* in the Sanskrit language means "Immovable" (*acala*) in Chinese;
*Bharadvāja* in the Sanskrit language means "Swift" (*javana*) in Chinese, which is his clan name. This Venerable One, together with a thousand...
The majority of Arhats reside on the continent of Aparagoyānī (in Sanskrit *Aparagoyānī*; in Chinese, *Gūyēní*, meaning "Cattle-Barter").
As for the Venerable Kāṇakavatsa (the Sanskrit *Kāṇakavatsa* has no equivalent translation), this venerable one and the majority of five hundred Arhats reside in the northern kingdom of Kaśmīra.
Regarding the Venerable Kanakavatsa (in Sanskrit: *Kanakavatsa*; no Chinese equivalent):
this venerable one, together with six hundred arhats, mostly resided on the continent of Pūrvavideha in the east.
Fourth is the Venerable Subhūti; *Subhūti* in Sanskrit has no equivalent translation [in Chinese].
This venerable one, together with seven hundred arhats, mostly resided in Uttarakuru.
Regarding the Venerable Nakula: *Nakula* in Sanskrit means "Mongoose Mountain.
This venerable one, together with eight hundred arhats, mostly resided on Jambudvīpa (Sanskrit; also called *Jambudvīpa*; Chinese: "Victorious Gold Island").
The Venerable Ṣaḍbhadra: in Sanskrit, *Ṣaḍbhadra*; in Chinese, "Good at Honoring the Worthy.
This venerable one, along with nine hundred arhats, mostly resided on the island of Tamradvīpa.
Seventh is the Venerable Kālika; in Sanskrit, *Kālika* (which has no equivalent translation).
This venerable one, along with many thousands of arhats, mostly resided on the continent of Saṃghāṭa.
As for the Venerable Vaśālavadana— Vaśālavadana in Sanskrit (which has no equivalent translation)—
this venerable one, together with one thousand one hundred arhats, mostly resided on the island of Pūrnadvīpa.
Regarding the Venerable Śubhaka: "Śubhaka" is the Sanskrit term (which has no direct Chinese equivalent).
This venerable one, together with nine hundred arhats, mostly resided on Mount Gandhamādana.
The Venerable Upārdhaka (the name *Upārdhaka* is untranslated in Chinese).
This venerable one, together with one thousand three hundred arhats, mostly resides in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (the Heaven of the Thirty-three is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven).
Eleventh is the Venerable Rāhula; in Sanskrit he is called Rāhula, which in the language of China means "Grasper of the Sun.
This venerable one, together with one thousand one hundred arhats, dwells for the most part on the continent of Pūrvavideha.
The Venerable Nāgasena, the twelfth [patriarch]— the Sanskrit term *nāgasena* has no direct equivalent in Chinese— this venerable one,
together with one thousand two hundred arhats, mostly resided on Mount Paṇḍava.
Thirteen: The Venerable Aṅgada. In the Sanskrit language, Aṅgada is untranslated [in Chinese].
This venerable one, together with one thousand three hundred arhats, mostly resided on Mount Vipula.
14. Vana-vāsin: The Venerable Vana-vāsin (the Sanskrit term *vana-vāsin* has no direct equivalent in Chinese).
This venerable one, together with one thousand four hundred arhats, mostly resided on Mount Kṛkavāku.
Fifteenth is the Venerable Āśvaghosa; "Āśvaghosa" in Sanskrit is untranslated [into Chinese].
This venerable one, together with fifteen hundred arhats, mostly resided on Vulture Peak Mountain.
16. The Venerable Cūḍapanthaka: In Sanskrit, *Cūḍapanthaka* (which has no direct equivalent in Chinese).
This venerable one, together with sixteen hundred arhats, mostly resided on Mount Dhurandhara.
